title: The famous story says the accident made him a different man. The record is thinner than that.
description:
The record is thinner than that. Malcolm Macmillan, who studied the case closely, says a personality change did occur but did not last much longer than two to three years.

Railroad foreman. On 13 September, near Cavendish, Vermont, a tamping iron went through his head. He was conscious and speaking within minutes.

And it went straight through. It entered below his left cheekbone, left through the top of his skull, and landed roughly 25 metres behind him.

Gage drove six-horse coaches on the Valparaiso to Santiago route. Macmillan reads his hiring as evidence that the worst changes were temporary.

'No longer Gage' was published in 1868. That was eight years after he died. Little was recorded about his personality before or after the accident.

The iron went through his head. The legend went further than the evidence.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phineas_Gage: read. Established the accident on 13 September 1848 near Cavendish, Vermont, while Gage was blasting rock as a railroad foreman; the tamping iron at 3 ft 7 in, 13¼ lb and 1¼ in across; its path under the left cheekbone and out of the top of the skull, landing about 80 ft (25 m) away; that he stayed conscious and spoke within minutes; the 1852 move to Chile to drive six-horse stagecoaches on the Valparaiso to Santiago route; his death on 21 May 1860; and Macmillan's argument that the 'no longer Gage' description was published in 1868, after his death, and that his later steady work undercuts the drifter story.
- https://www.npr.org/transcripts/528966102: read. Corroborated the date, the 13 lb iron, Gage's age of 25 and his work as a railroad foreman, the stagecoach job in Chile, and quoted Malcolm Macmillan saying a personality change 'undoubtedly occurred' but 'did not last much longer than about two to three years'.
- https://www.britannica.com/print/article/1940849: read. Corroborated the date, the iron at 13.25 lb and 1.25 in across, the exit through the top of the skull, that he was conscious and could speak straight after, the 1852 Chile coaching job, his death in May 1860 from seizures nearly 12 years later, and that little was recorded about his personality before or after, so the extent of any change is unknown.
